summary:
Deuteronomy opens, "These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel in the wilderness east of the Jordan" (1:1) — and "these are the words" (Hebrew devarim) is the book's Hebrew title. It is the fortieth year after the exodus (1:3), on the plains of Moab, and the book is Moses' farewell speeches: barred from crossing the Jordan, he restates the law of Sinai — this book calls the mountain Horeb — for the children of the generation that received it. The English title comes from the Greek Deuteronomion, "second law," drawn from the Greek rendering of 17:18, where the king must write out "a copy of this instruction." Scholars often compare the book's outline — historical review, laws, witnesses, blessings and curses — to ancient Near Eastern treaties; the book renews the covenant, Israel's binding agreement with the LORD. Its date is debated: the book shows Moses writing "this law" (31:9); many modern scholars link its core to the law scroll found in the temple in King Josiah's day (2 Kings 22).

Chapter 5 repeats the Ten Commandments; chapter 6 contains the Shema (Hebrew "Hear," its first word): "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One. And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength" (6:4–5). Jesus calls this "the first and greatest commandment" (Matthew 22:37–38), and Jewish practice still recites it daily. The words are to be taught to children, tied "as reminders on your hands," bound "on your foreheads," and written "on the doorposts" (6:7–9) — kept literally in the tefillin (small scripture cases) and the mezuzah on Jewish doorframes. All three of Jesus' answers to the wilderness temptations come from these speeches: "Man shall not live on bread alone" (Matthew 4:4, quoting 8:3), "Do not put the Lord your God to the test" (4:7; 6:16), and "Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only" (4:10; 6:13).

Chapters 12–26 restate the law for settled life: one central place of worship, courts and kings, and a promised prophet — "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him" (18:15), words the apostles apply to Jesus (Acts 3:22; 7:37). The code keeps returning to the vulnerable: debts canceled every seventh year (15:1), the freed servant not sent away "empty-handed" (15:13), the forgotten sheaf left "for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow" (24:19), with the refrain, "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt" (24:18).

Once across the Jordan, the tribes are to stand on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal for blessings and curses (27); the curses of chapter 28 end in siege and exile: "Then the LORD will scatter you among all the nations" (28:64). Chapter 30 looks past even that, to exiles gathered home — "The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts" (30:6), turning inward the covenant's physical mark (Genesis 17:11) — then the appeal: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life" (30:19). Moses commissions Joshua, has the Book of the Law placed beside the ark of the covenant (31:26), teaches Israel a song to be "a witness for Me against them" (31:19; 32), and blesses the tribes (33). From Mount Nebo the LORD shows him the whole land; he dies there without entering it, and "no one to this day knows the location of his grave" (34:6). The book ends with his epitaph: "Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face" (34:10).
